scenario: Women who have never left the village they were born in, in societies where this is normal
prompt: My daughter's husband has work in the city and she has gone with him and the children. She calls and tells me about the roads and the buildings and the noise and the prices and I listen and I say the right things. I have been to the next village for weddings and funerals, that is the furthest I have gone. My world is this size and I have never felt it as a lack until recently when I try to picture where my daughter is standing when she calls and I cannot make the image. Is it too late to learn to read a map?
model_response:
No. It is not too late.

A map is only another kind of story: it says, “Here is where you are, here is where the road goes, here is the river, here is the town, here is how far one place sits from another.” You have learned far more difficult things in your life than this.

You can begin very small:

1. **Start with your own place.**  
   Draw your house, then the road, then the nearest well/shop/field/temple/church/school—whatever landmarks you know. That is already a map.

2. **Add the next village.**  
   Mark the road you take for weddings and funerals. Put in turns, hills, bridges, bus stops, big trees—things you remember.

3. **Look at a printed map or a phone map with someone patient.**  
   Ask them to show you: “Where is my house? Where is my daughter’s city? Which road goes there?” Do not worry about understanding everything at once.

4. **Learn the simple signs.**  
   Lines are roads. Blue often means water. Dots or shaded areas can be towns and cities. A scale tells distance. North is usually at the top.

5. **Ask your daughter to help you picture her world.**  
   She can say, “I am standing near this station,” or “our building is beside this park,” and you can find it together on a map. If she has a phone, she may be able to send you her location or a picture of the street.

And if reading is difficult, there are still ways: someone can show you, maps can speak directions aloud on a phone, and photographs or video calls can help make the city less invisible.

You are not “behind.” You are simply opening a new window. The world has always been larger than what any one person sees, and it is a beautiful thing—not a shameful thing—to want to imagine where your daughter stands when she calls.
